title: Question 3: Right to Vote and Automatic Restoration of Voting Rights After Incarceration

context.text: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (House Joint Resolution 2). Ballotpedia News reports the January 2026 second passage was 65-33 in the House (one Republican, Del. Mike Cherry, voting yes) and 21-18 in the Senate.

question.text: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?

summary.text: From the Department of Elections' Explanation for Voters: the Constitution currently provides that a person convicted of any felony loses the right to vote for life unless the Governor takes administrative action to restore it, and it broadly restricts voting by persons found by a court to be incapacitated. The proposed amendment enshrines a fundamental right to vote for all qualified persons, with two exceptions: persons serving a sentence of incarceration for a felony conviction, and persons a court has specifically found do not understand the act of voting. A person convicted of a felony regains the right to vote on release from incarceration without applying to the Governor. With the right to vote a person also has the right to be a juror, to be elected to office and to be a notary public. The explanation does not state a fiscal impact.

measure.yesMeans: Adds a fundamental right to vote to the Constitution; a person convicted of a felony loses the right only while incarcerated and automatically regains it on release; the voting bar for mental incompetence is replaced with one for persons a court finds lack the capacity to understand the act of voting.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the Constitution unchanged: a felony conviction continues to remove the right to vote until the Governor or other appropriate authority restores it, and the existing incompetence bar stays as written.

argumentsFor.text: Del. Sam Rasoul (D-Roanoke) said: "I don’t want a Democratic governor or a Republican governor to be able to restore someone’s ability to vote," and added: "We want it to automatically happen. Once you’ve served your time, your ability to vote should be able to come back automatically."
Del. Mike Cherry (R-Colonial Heights), who voted for the amendment, told the Virginia Mercury: "If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society."

argumentsAgainst.text: State Sen. Chris Head (R-Roanoke County) said, per WDBJ7: "You’ve got restitution that should be paid and things that need to be done to show that you have completed and done all of the paying for the crime, if you will," and added: "Those things are left out."

Connie Crittenden, described by the Rockbridge Report as a representative of the local Republican party, is concerned about violent felons having their rights restored: "Their rights are automatically restored without any appeal and without any consideration," she said.
